result: The study recruited 59,571 qualified participants from around the world through the MindCrowd online platform. The sample was 62.46% female and 37.54% male, predominantly White (92.03%), with varying education levels and 22.76% reporting family history of Alzheimer's disease.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the impressive sample size of ~60,000 people as a strength of the study, stating it 'permits a well-powered exploration of factors.' The demographic characteristics were not questioned, though reviewers did note the sample was 'predominantly White' and requested clarification about socioeconomic status (SES) as a potential confounding factor.

result: Age was significantly associated with PAL performance (BAge = −0.20 word pairs, pAge <2e-16), with performance declining by approximately two word-pairs per decade of life.
evaluation: Reviewers questioned the linear relationship between age and PAL performance, noting it 'seems not to be in agreement with findings of memory decline across age which is not described by linear functions but a sinuous curve (cf. Jack et al. on dynamics in AD development).' They requested the authors comment on this discrepancy.

result: Women showed significantly higher PAL scores compared to men (BSex = −1.82, pSex <2e-16), with nearly a two word-pair advantage. The sex disparity markedly increased around the 5th decade of life, growing from the 5th to 6th decade (50s: 2.68ATT ±0.35 SD-word pairs, 60s: 3.72ATT ±0.32 SD-word pairs). This represents the first demonstration of the sex-effect for PAL across the entire adult lifespan in a large cohort using the same test.
evaluation: Reviewers found the sex-differences 'particularly interesting,' especially the discussion around the 5th decade in relation to menopause and estrogen effects. However, they questioned the 'somewhat arbitrary age cut-off point of 65 years,' suggesting the authors may 'conceal important hormonally-driven transitions in cognitive function in women' and asked if it's possible to examine these factors earlier in the lifespan.

result: Educational attainment was a significant predictor of PAL scores (BEducation = 0.31, pEducation <2e-16), with each milestone associated with approximately one-third of a word pair higher score. The education effect differed by sex, with women showing higher PAL scores related to education than men at all except the highest level (16y vs. 20y).
evaluation: Reviewers did not directly critique the education findings but raised concerns about socioeconomic status (SES) as a potential confounding variable, noting that 'educational attainment, dietary/medical risk factors, alcohol/drug consumption, diabetes, and even family history of AD may all relate to, or interact with, lower SES.' They requested SES be included as a covariate if possible.

result: Family history of Alzheimer's disease showed a significant main effect on PAL performance (BFH = −2.39, pFH = 3.47e-06), with FH+ participants showing nearly 2.5 word-pairs lower scores. There was a significant Age x FH interaction (BAge*FH = 0.02, pAge*FH <0.01), with FH effects only observed in participants ≤65 years old, representing reduced PAL performance four decades before typical AD onset.
evaluation: Reviewers identified this as 'the most significant finding' but raised substantial concerns about how FH was defined and measured. They requested 'exact wording' for the FH measure, clarification about whether it included all family members or only first-degree relatives, and whether it distinguished between sporadic and familial AD. They also questioned the validity and reliability of self-reported FH data, requesting details about 'age of onset, specific symptom profiles, whether there was functional decline.'

result: There was a significant Sex x FH interaction (BSex*FH = −0.79, pSex*FH = 7.97e-06), with FH+ men showing greater reduction in PAL scores compared to FH+ women. The estimated word pair reduction was larger in men (20s: ATT1.93 ±SD0.60) compared to women (20s: ATT0.60 ±SD0.67), except in the 6th decade of life.
evaluation: Reviewers noted this finding that 'FH men showed a greater reduction in cognition compared to FH women' as part of the significant findings. However, the concerns about FH definition and measurement reliability apply to this interaction as well.

result: There was a significant Educational Attainment x FH interaction (BEducation*FH = 0.08, pEducation*FH <0.01), with FH associated with lower PAL scores at each education milestone. The magnitude of FH-related decline was greater at lower education levels (12y difference = 1.6) compared to higher levels (20y difference = 1.2).
evaluation: While reviewers did not directly critique this interaction, their concerns about SES as a confounding variable are particularly relevant here, as they noted 'educational attainment... may all relate to, or interact with, lower SES' and that SES 'might be a common underlying variable that modulates the risk for cognitive decline.'

result: There was a significant FH x Diabetes interaction (BFH*Diabetes = −0.71, pFH*Diabetes = 0.04), with FH+ participants with diabetes showing lower PAL scores (EMM = 16.9) compared to FH+ participants without diabetes (EMM = 18.1, t(53763) = 2.73, p=0.03).
evaluation: Reviewers did not directly critique the diabetes findings, though they noted concern that 'the potential role of other risk factors/disease does not appear to have been taken into account' and requested clarification or acknowledgment as a limitation.

result: In FH+ participants, there was a significant main effect for number of APOE ε4 alleles (Bε4Allele = −1.30, pε4Allele = 0.02), with approximately 1.3 word-pairs lower PAL score per ε4 allele in a dose-dependent manner. FH+ participants with ε4-ε4 genotype showed five word-pairs lower scores compared to ε2-ε3 genotype (Bε4-ε4 vs.ε2-ε3 = −5.32, pε4-ε4 vs.ε2-ε3 = 0.03).
evaluation: Reviewers identified 'the inclusion of APOE genotype data in a large subgroup' as 'a further strength of the study.' They did not raise specific concerns about the APOE findings themselves, accepting the dose-dependent relationship and genotype comparisons.

result: Error simulation analysis showed that with 8% additional introduced error in FH self-report, the study could demonstrate statistically significant effect of FH on PAL in 100% of 10,000 tested iterations. Even with 24% additional error, the effect remained significant in over 50% of iterations, suggesting FH self-report error is unlikely to be driving the significant effect.
evaluation: While the authors conducted error simulation, reviewers fundamentally questioned 'the validity and reliability' of self-reported data regarding FH and lifestyle conditions, stating these data 'are not presented.' They requested details about how questions were phrased, coded, and whether answers 'might be interpreted and responded to differently across cultures/languages.' The simulation does not fully address these concerns about systematic bias versus random error.

result: PAL was tested cross-sectionally in the cohort, making it impossible to determine the influence of collected factors on trajectories of change in performance across time within individual subjects.
evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly critique the cross-sectional design as a limitation, implicitly accepting this methodological constraint. The authors appropriately acknowledged this limitation.

result: The study demonstrates the utility of web-based cohort recruitment, with the advantage of considerably larger sample sizes and enriched cohort diversity mostly diminishing potential disadvantages of online research.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the 'impressive' sample size of ~60,000 people as a strength that 'permits a well-powered exploration of factors.' However, they also raised concerns about self-report reliability and potential selection bias in web-based studies, though they did not fundamentally reject the approach.

result: The 5th decade of life is when women undergo menopause in developed countries, and menopause-related hormonal changes have been found to alter cognition during this period.
evaluation: Reviewers found this discussion 'particularly interesting,' noting that 'Estrogen has been suggested to offer a neuroprotective effect.' They requested further exploration of whether 'sharp declines in PAL performance are evident in women from the 6th decade onwards (when presumably hormonal levels are much lower, and hysterectomy may have occurred).'

result: Socioeconomic status (SES) has been shown to have associations with brain structure, cognitive measures during development, and may play a role in AD risk.
evaluation: Reviewers identified the omission of SES as 'not a trivial omission,' noting that 'a number of the factors of interest could potentially be explained by lower SES' including 'educational attainment, dietary/medical risk factors, alcohol/drug consumption, diabetes, and even family history of AD.' They requested SES be included as a covariate if possible, or at minimum acknowledged as a limitation.
